items.title: Belkin’s kid-friendly wireless headphones are 25 percent off
items.raw:
The SoundForm Mini 2 come in a variety of colors, and include a carrying case if you’re willing to spend a bit more. | Image: The Verge	

Verge readers can get a discount on Belkin’s SoundForm Mini 2 wireless headphones. The kid-focused on-ear headphones feature an 85-decibel volume limit and easy controls, and a mode that lets them beam audio (wired or wirelessly) to a second pair without extra hardware. Readers can use the code VERGE25OFF to save 25 percent on up to two pairs of SoundForm Mini 2 headphones.
The $29.99 model without the zip-up carrying case gets knocked down to $22.49. Alternatively, a more limited selection of colors are currently available that include a case, which is $29.99 instead of $39.99 once the offer code is applied in the cart.
Belkin SoundForm Mini 2 headphones

Where to Buy:

 $29.99 $22.49 at Belkin (without carrying case)
 $39.99 $29.99 at Belkin (with carrying case)

While these don’t deliver noise cancellation, they should be good enough for most situations. They can last up to 55 hours on a single change, and they can fold up neatly to fit into a variety of bags. The SoundForm Mini 2 are made for ages 3 and up, and feature an adjustable headband and cushioned earcups. They’re pretty no-frills, though the audio-sharing mode I described above is a great way around having to buy some sort of audio splitter or wireless transmitter to ensure multiple kids are entertained.

Onto more capable headphones, the Sonos Ace have been succeeded by the $449 Ace Ultra that offer better battery life, improved noise cancellation, plus the feature we most wished was in the original: the ability to directly link them to speakers via Wi-Fi, letting you move freely around your home instead of close to your soundbar. Those are sizable improvements, but the original Sonos Ace is still a fantastic value, especially at the current $299.99 sale price from Amazon and Best Buy. While not a new discount, it’s nice to have a lower-cost alternative available. In our 2024 review, we bemoaned the iffy state of the Sonos app, and criticized the Ace for not working with the Beam and Ray soundbars for TV Audio Swap. The company recently debuted its plans for overhauling the app, and TV Audio Swap support for those soundbars has been added following their debut.
Kirby Air Riders for the Nintendo Switch 2 is close to $20 off for the physical version at Amazon, which is its lowest price yet. You can snag it for $51.99, while the digital version is still selling for $69.99. While not an essential Switch 2 title for those building out their libraries with a limited budget, it delivers F-Zero-esque frenzy that Mario Kart World can’t match. It’s the follow-up to Kirby Air Ride on the GameCube, giving players more flexibility in who they race as, what aircraft they use, plus a host of game modes to give you more to do than just racing. Read our review.
If you’re in the mood to shop, but you’re not quite sure what you want, it might be worth taking a spin through the Amazon Resale catalog of returned products. Many products are marked down by up to 30 percent once you add them to your cart. Just look for the green “Save at checkout” on product listings where Amazon Resale is the seller. The percentage of savings differs per product. I didn’t find any earthshaking deals on consoles or other big-ticket items, but you can save a good amount on things like controllers and headphones.

items.title: Almost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts find
items.raw:
Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities
Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.
Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.

items.title: UK must end all trade with Israel, says co-founder of BDS movement
items.raw:
Exclusive: sanctions against ministers and settler groups are ‘smoke and mirrors cop-out’ says Omar Barghouti
Britain’s legal and ethical obligation to stop a genocide in Gaza requires it to take bigger steps than halting trade with illegal Israeli settlements or imposing further sanctions, Omar Barghouti, the co-founder of the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) movement has said.
He described sanctions against individual settler groups or extremist ministers as a “smoke and mirrors cop-out and distraction” from the UK’s legal obligation under international law to end all support for Israel, including arms exports, trade deals and academic relations that “may directly or indirectly enable Israel’s illegal occupation” of Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem.

The new limit, which went into effect on Tuesday, applies to residential roads with no centre line or maximum speed signs, media reports said.

items.title: South African airline defends dramatic low-level flyby before rugby union clash
items.raw:
Cape Town stunt sparks major debate over safety risks

Airlink insists flyby conducted according to regulations

A pre-game stunt involving two passenger jets flying dramatically low over a stadium in South Africa drew huge cheers from the estimated crowd of 56,000 people, but also sparked a major debate over safety risks. The flyby by two Embraer jets, operated by the local airline Airlink, happened on Saturday before the second rugby union Test between South Africa and New Zealand in Cape Town.
The flight tracking service Flightradar24 estimated that the lead jet passed just 41-46 feet (12-14 metres) above the roof of Cape Town Stadium, with the crowd and the world’s top-ranked rugby teams below. The second jet, which was very close behind, flew through a cloud of pink dust that shot up from the stadium roof as part of the show.

Guidance says states must implement ‘comprehensive measures’ to address legacy of racial discrimination
A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.
Guidance published on Monday by the committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD) said the obligations arose from ⁠a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place.

As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter the Spanish enclave at the end of July. The influx of about 70,000 men, women and children unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.
